candidates.quote: They do come to you; but you do not hear them. You have not sat in the field in the evening listening for them. When the angelus rings you cross yourself and have done with it; but if you prayed from your heart, and listened to the thrilling of the bells in the air after they stop ringing, you would hear the voices as well as I do.
candidates.author: Bernard Shaw
candidates.locator: scene V, in the ambulatory of Rheims cathedral after the coronation, Joan answering Charles when he asks why the voices never come to him; read verbatim in the Project Gutenberg Australia text of the play, which prints Shaw's unapostrophed dont in Charles's line just above
candidates.speaker: Joan
candidates.whyThisMonth: It says plainly what the month is for: the voices are not withheld, they are unheard, and the cure is sitting still in a field long enough to hear the bells go on after they stop.

candidates.quote: Thou hast come to a steed-famed land for rest, / O stranger worn with toil, / To a land of all lands the goodliest / Colonus’ glistening soil.
candidates.author: Sophocles
candidates.locator: the first strophe of the Colonus ode, from line 668, sung by the Chorus to the exhausted Oedipus; read verbatim in Storr's English in the Project Gutenberg Oedipus Trilogy, where the verse does not run line for line with the Greek lineation, so the four lines are the opening of Storr's stanza
candidates.speaker: the Chorus
candidates.whyThisMonth: The oldest welcome in the theatre is offered to a man who has walked too far, and it offers him nothing but a quiet place and permission to stop.

candidates.quote: I pray the gods to quit me of my toils, / To close the watch I keep, this livelong year; / For as a watch-dog lying, not at rest, / Propped on one arm, upon the palace-roof / Of Atreus’ race, too long, too well I know / The starry conclave of the midnight sky.
candidates.author: Aeschylus
candidates.locator: the Watchman's opening speech, the first six lines of Morshead's English in The House of Atreus, read verbatim in the Project Gutenberg text; the sentence runs on past line six, so the full stop marks a cut at a complete clause
candidates.speaker: the Watchman
candidates.whyThisMonth: European drama opens with a man who has been awake and alone on a roof all night, and the honest reward of that vigil is that he now knows the whole sky by heart.

candidates.quote: Why, yes, it is Sunday every day, in every house, when people open their eyes.
candidates.author: Maurice Maeterlinck
candidates.locator: Act IV, scene 2, the Palace of Happiness, the Happiness of Being Well answering Tyltyl; read verbatim in the Teixeira de Mattos text on Project Gutenberg, where Maeterlinck closes the sentence with his four dots, so the full stop here stands in for his ellipsis
candidates.speaker: the Happiness of Being Well
candidates.whyThisMonth: A whole play of searching ends in the discovery that the ordinary morning was already the thing looked for, which is the kindest possible thing to hear at six.

candidates.quote: Now we will count to twelve / and we will all keep still.
candidates.author: Pablo Neruda
candidates.locator: the opening two lines of A callarse in Extravagaria, 1958, in Reid's English, given as pages 27 to 29 of the 1974 Farrar, Straus and Giroux volume; HEDGE: the page was not opened, and the lineation and the lower case and at the head of line two rest on two independent reprints that credit Reid
candidates.whyThisMonth: It is the month's instruction in two lines: not silence forever, only twelve counts of it, which anyone can manage before the day starts.

candidates.quote: And I shall have some peace there, for peace comes dropping slow, / Dropping from the veils of the morning to where the cricket sings; / There midnight’s all a glimmer, and noon a purple glow, / And evening full of the linnet’s wings.
candidates.author: W. B. Yeats
candidates.locator: the second stanza, lines 5 to 8, read verbatim in the Project Gutenberg text of Yeats's Poems; first printed in the National Observer, 13 December 1890, and collected in The Rose
candidates.whyThisMonth: Peace here is not decided on, it falls, slowly and from the morning downward, which is the right speed for a reader who has just woken.

candidates.quote: Till rising and gliding out I wander’d off by myself, / In the mystical moist night-air, and from time to time, / Look’d up in perfect silence at the stars.
candidates.author: Walt Whitman
candidates.work: When I Heard the Learn’d Astronomer
candidates.locator: the closing three lines, in Book XX, By the Roadside, of Leaves of Grass; read verbatim in the Project Gutenberg text of the 1891 to 1892 edition, which prints the elided wander’d and Look’d
candidates.whyThisMonth: It gives the reader permission to leave the lecture and simply look, and it names the thing this month is after: perfect silence, out of doors, with something overhead.

candidates.quote: Thousands at his bidding speed / And post o’re Land and Ocean without rest: / They also serve who only stand and waite.
candidates.author: John Milton
candidates.work: When I consider how my light is spent
candidates.locator: the closing three lines, lines 12 to 14; the sonnet is numbered XVI in the Poems of 1673 and XIX in later editions; read verbatim in Beeching's Oxford text of 1900, which keeps the old spellings o’re and waite
candidates.whyThisMonth: For anyone who wakes already behind, it sets the thousands who rush beside the ones who only stand, and refuses to rank them.

candidates.quote: Watching the moon / at dawn, / solitary, mid-sky, / I knew myself completely, / no part left out.
candidates.author: Izumi Shikibu
candidates.locator: one of the Izumi Shikibu poems in Hirshfield and Aratani's volume, 1988; HEDGE: the page was not opened, and the reading matters, because Hirshfield's later anthology Women in Praise of the Sacred prints at midnight where The Ink Dark Moon prints at dawn, so the volume must be named on the card
candidates.whyThisMonth: Five lines of a woman awake at first light, alone, and the reward of that stillness is not insight about the moon but a whole sight of herself.

candidates.quote: Some time now past in the Autumnal Tide, / When Phœbus wanted but one hour to bed, / The trees all richly clad, yet void of pride, / Where gilded o’re by his rich golden head.
candidates.author: Anne Bradstreet
candidates.locator: stanza 1, lines 1 to 4, in Several Poems, Boston, 1678; read verbatim in the Ellis edition of 1867, which follows the 1678 sheets: Where in line four is the old spelling of Were, and modern editions emend it
candidates.whyThisMonth: A woman steps out at the end of an October day and simply looks at the trees, and the poem's whole long argument starts from that one act of looking.

candidates.quote: Up the dome of heaven / Like a great hill, / I watch them marching / Stately and still, / And I know that I / Am honored to be / Witness / Of so much majesty.
candidates.author: Sara Teasdale
candidates.locator: the last two stanzas, lines 17 to 24, in Flame and Shadow, Macmillan, 1920; read verbatim in the Project Gutenberg text, whose alternating indents are not reproducible in a single line
candidates.whyThisMonth: It names the only job a person has when standing still under a sky: to be a witness, which is a task anyone can do before breakfast.

candidates.quote: I don’t know exactly what a prayer is. / I do know how to pay attention, how to fall down / into the grass, how to kneel down in the grass, / how to be idle and blessed, how to stroll through the fields, / which is what I have been doing all day.
candidates.author: Mary Oliver
candidates.locator: lines 11 to 15, in House of Light, Beacon Press, 1990; HEDGE: the page was not opened, and the line numbering follows a standard study text of the poem, so the five line breaks must be checked against the Beacon printing
candidates.whyThisMonth: It lets a reader off the hook about prayer and hands back something plainer and harder: attention, idleness, and a whole day spent on them without apology.

candidates.quote: Let it come, as it will, and don’t / be afraid. God does not leave us / comfortless, so let evening come.
candidates.author: Jane Kenyon
candidates.locator: the final stanza, lines 16 to 18, from Let Evening Come, Graywolf Press, 1990; the lineation here is the one poets.org prints, crediting the text of Otherwise: New and Selected Poems, 1996
candidates.whyThisMonth: A poem built entirely of small things settling into their places ends by telling the reader not to be afraid of the quiet that is coming.

candidates.quote: We call it a grain of sand, / but it calls itself neither grain nor sand.
candidates.author: Wisława Szymborska
candidates.work: View with a Grain of Sand
candidates.locator: the opening two lines; the Polish poem is in Ludzie na moście, 1986, and this English is from View with a Grain of Sand: Selected Poems, Harcourt Brace, 1995; HEDGE: the page was not opened, and the first stanza's wording rests on reprints that credit Barańczak and Cavanagh
candidates.whyThisMonth: It is the quietest possible correction: the world is going about its business without our names for it, and noticing that is the beginning of paying attention.

candidates.quote: Evening, all things thou bringest / Which dawn spread apart from each other; / The lamb and the kid thou bringest, / Thou bringest the boy to his mother.
candidates.author: Sappho
candidates.locator: fragment 95 in Wharton's numbering, 104a in Lobel and Page; the rendering by J. A. Symonds, 1883, as printed in Wharton's Sappho: Memoir, Text, Selected Renderings and a Literal Translation, third edition, John Lane, 1895, read verbatim in the Project Gutenberg text
candidates.whyThisMonth: The oldest lyric about evening is simply a list of things coming home, which is what stillness is for: gathering back what the day scattered.

candidates.quote: Earth’s crammed with heaven, / And every common bush afire with God: / But only he who sees, takes off his shoes.
candidates.author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
candidates.locator: the Seventh Book, in Aurora's speech on the double vision, the lines usually cited as VII.820 following; read verbatim in the Project Gutenberg text, which prints a colon after God and a semicolon after shoes, so the full stop marks a cut at a complete clause before The rest sit round it
candidates.whyThisMonth: It divides the world not into sacred and ordinary places but into people who look and people who do not, and it makes looking the whole of the work.
